| Spirometry with bronchodilator | Is there airflow obstruction and is it reversible? | FEV₁/FVC < 0.7 with ≥12 % and ≥200 mL rise in FEV₁ after SABA → supports asthma; lack of reversibility suggests COPD or fixed disease |
Consider if the patient is systemically unwell, very frail, has comorbidity (COPD, heart failure), or pertussis is suspected (macrolide).
Secondary spontaneous: Underlying lung disease: COPD (commonest), TB, PCP (HIV), cystic fibrosis, asthma, lung cancer, ILD, Marfan syndrome, catamenial (menstrual)
Differential: COPD, heart failure ("cardiac asthma"), GORD, vocal cord dysfunction, bronchiectasis, foreign body, PE.
Spirometry (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 = COPD); chest X-ray (increased bronchovascular markings, to exclude other causes); sputum culture in exacerbations; FBC (polycythaemia), ABG.

qs.q: Which of the following best characterizes the airflow limitation seen in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)?
o: Completely reversible following treatment with inhaled short-acting beta-agonists
Persistent and not fully reversible, with progressive airflow limitation over time
Present only during acute viral infections and resolves entirely between episodes
Fixed airway obstruction that responds normally and fully to salbutamol
qs.e: COPD is defined by persistent airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, though it may improve slightly with salbutamol. Fully reversible airflow limitation is more characteristic of asthma rather than COPD.

qs.q: Which of the following systemic manifestations or complications is typically associated with advanced COPD?
o: Polycythemia with persistent metabolic alkalosis and compensatory respiratory acidosis
Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis as compensation
Severe acute metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation from muscle fatigue
Normal acid-base status due to complete renal compensation for chronic hypoxia
qs.e: COPD leads to chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis as a compensatory mechanism. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis is not the typical compensation pattern described.

qs.q: A patient with suspected COPD is noted on physical examination to have prominent finger clubbing. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this physical sign?
o: Finger clubbing is a classic expected sign of uncomplicated advanced COPD
Finger clubbing is not a feature of COPD and should prompt exclusion of lung cancer, fibrosis, or bronchiectasis
Finger clubbing indicates severe cor pulmonale and right-sided heart failure
Finger clubbing confirms the presence of pan-acinar emphysema due to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
qs.e: Finger clubbing is not a feature of COPD and should trigger further investigation for alternative diagnoses such as lung cancer, bronchiectasis, or fibrosis. It is therefore an important red flag during clinical evaluation.

qs.q: Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms directly contributes to air trapping and hyperinflation in COPD?
o: Increased elastic recoil of the lung parenchyma during inspiration
Loss of elasticity and alveolar attachments of airways due to emphysema causing collapse during expiration
Bronchial smooth muscle relaxation leading to excessive widening of small air passages
Destruction of the pulmonary capillary bed without any changes to airway caliber
qs.e: Loss of elastic recoil and alveolar attachments due to emphysema causes airways to collapse during expiration, resulting in air trapping and hyperinflation. Increased elastic recoil would prevent rather than promote airway collapse.

qs.q: Which of the following extrapulmonary systemic components is frequently seen as a consequence of systemic inflammation in COPD?
o: Rapid and sustained weight gain due to glucocorticoid receptor hypersensitivity
Muscle weakness and cachexia driven by catabolic effects of inflammatory markers like CRP and TNF
Marked osteoblast activation leading to high bone mineral density and thick bones
Enhanced salt and water excretion resulting in chronic profound dehydration
qs.e: Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein, TNF, and interleukins exert a catabolic effect on both muscle and bone, contributing to muscle weakness, cachexia, and osteoporosis. They impair rather than enhance salt and water excretion.

qs.q: What is the most common early symptom of COPD that patients often manage by adopting a sedentary lifestyle to avoid?
o: Exertional dyspnea
Painless hemoptysis
Nocturnal orthopnea
High-pitched inspiratory stridor
qs.e: Exertional dyspnea is the most common early symptom of COPD, which sedentary patients may unconsciously avoid by limiting physical activity. Hemoptysis and stridor are not the typical hallmark early complaints.

qs.q: Which percussion finding is classically elicited in a patient with significant hyperinflation due to COPD?
o: Dullness over the lung bases due to pleural effusions
Hyperresonance because the lungs are hyperinflated with air
Stony dullness throughout the anterior chest wall
Normal resonant percussion note with reduced diaphragmatic excursion
qs.e: Percussion of the chest in COPD typically reveals hyperresonance because the lungs are hyperinflated with trapped air. Dullness would indicate consolidation or pleural fluid rather than hyperinflation.

qs.q: Global epidemiological data cited regarding COPD indicate which of the following regarding its mortality burden?
o: It was the leading cause of death worldwide by the year 2000
By 2020, it is forecast to represent the third most important cause of death worldwide
It accounts for less than one percent of all global mortalities in developing countries
It is projected to drop below all infectious respiratory diseases in mortality rank by 2030
qs.e: The notes explicitly state that by 2020, COPD is forecast to represent the third most important cause of death worldwide. It ranks behind cardiovascular and other major categories before reaching that specific milestone.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: COPD is a progressive lung disease causing airflow limitation. It's primarily linked to smoking and environmental irritants. Management focuses on symptom relief, reducing exacerbations, and slowing disease progression.

sections.p: COPD is a progressive, largely irreversible airflow limitation, often associated with chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Diagnosis is suspected in patients with chronic respiratory symptoms and a history of exposure to noxious particles, especially smoking. Spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 confirms the diagnosis.
b: Symptoms include chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnoea.
A history of significant exposure to risk factors is crucial.

sections.p: Severity is assessed by symptom burden, exacerbation frequency, and spirometric findings. The GOLD system categorises COPD into stages based on FEV1 and symptom scores (CAT or mMRC).

The most common cause is long-term exposure to cigarette smoke. Other significant causes include biomass fuel exposure (indoor air pollution), occupational dusts and chemicals, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Patients typically present with chronic cough, often worse in the morning, sputum production, and progressive shortness of breath, especially on exertion. Exacerbations are acute worsening of symptoms.

t.b: Confirms airflow limitation and aids diagnosis. A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.7 indicates COPD.
Excludes other causes of symptoms like pneumonia or lung cancer. May show hyperinflation or flattened diaphragms in COPD.
Assesses oxygenation and ventilation, especially in moderate to severe COPD or during exacerbations. Hypoxia and hypercapnia may be present.

sections.p: Acute exacerbations, pneumothorax, pneumonia, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, and respiratory failure are serious complications. A sudden increase in dyspnoea or chest pain warrants urgent assessment.

Management aims to reduce symptoms, decrease exacerbation frequency, and improve exercise tolerance. Smoking cessation is the most effective intervention. Pharmacological treatment includes bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids. Pulmonary rehabilitation is vital.
Regular follow-up is essential to monitor disease progression, adjust treatment, and manage exacerbations. Prevention focuses on smoking cessation and avoiding exposure to irritants.
COPD can be mistaken for asthma, heart failure, bronchiectasis, and interstitial lung disease due to overlapping symptoms like dyspnoea and cough.
Spirometry may be normal in very early disease. ABGs can appear normal at rest in patients with moderate COPD, only showing abnormalities with exertion or during exacerbations.
b: Normal ABGs at rest in stable COPD
Pulse oximetry may not reflect severe hypoxemia in some cases.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of shortness of breath
Bluish discoloration of lips or face

faq.q: What is the main cause of COPD?
faq.a: The most common cause is long-term exposure to cigarette smoke.
COPD cannot be cured, but its progression can be slowed and symptoms managed effectively.

faq.q: What is an exacerbation of COPD?
faq.a: An exacerbation is a sudden worsening of COPD symptoms, often requiring increased medication or hospitalization.
